Grok's response (as captured)

Treating the fragment as a three-line system next to the sandbox metric 2xc−d=12xc - d = 12xc−d=1:

Fmc′⋅1d=f\frac{Fmc' \cdot 1}{d} = fdFmc′⋅1​=f
∗c=d−1\ast c = d - 1∗c=d−1
c=fc = fc=f

From the last line, f=cf = cf=c.

From the middle line, d=∗c+1d = \ast c + 1d=∗c+1.

The standing metric requires d=2xc−1d = 2xc - 1d=2xc−1, so the two expressions for ddd agree only when

∗c+1=2xc−1  ⇒  ∗c=2xc−2.\ast c + 1 = 2xc - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \ast c = 2xc - 2.∗c+1=2xc−1⇒∗c=2xc−2.

That holds for a specific pair (x,c)(x, c)(x,c), not in general. The usual consistent assignment is the opposite sign:

d=2xc−1i.e.∗c=d+1(with ∗=2x).d = 2xc - 1 \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \ast c = d + 1 \qquad (\text{with } \ast = 2x).d=2xc−1i.e.∗c=d+1(with ∗=2x).

If the intent is to keep the metric and set c=fc = fc=f, pick any x,cx, cx,c and lock

d=2xc−1,f=c.d = 2xc - 1, \qquad f = c.d=2xc−1,f=c.

Example that satisfies everything except the written d−1d - 1d−1:

x=1,c=1,d=1,f=1.x = 1, \quad c = 1, \quad d = 1, \quad f = 1.x=1,c=1,d=1,f=1.

If you meant a different operator for ∗\ast∗ or for the prime on Fmc, send the intended expansion and the numbers can be re-solved.
